sections.h2: How is property tax figured on a Tennessee house?
sections.html:
Tennessee takes the appraised value of the house, applies a fixed percentage set by state law, and multiplies the result by the local tax rate. For a residence the percentage is 25 percent. The Comptroller's tax bill page lists four parts: appraised value, assessment ratio, assessed value and tax rate.

Here is a worked example with round numbers. A house appraised at $240,000 has an assessed value of $60,000. If the combined rate is $2.80 per $100 of assessed value, the bill is $60,000 divided by 100, times 2.80, or $1,680. The rate itself comes from the county commission, and from a city governing body if the home sits inside city limits.

Tax amounts are not a valid reason to appeal. The Comptroller's guide to assessment and taxation says an appeal must rest on a value that is too high, another owner's value that is too low, or the wrong classification. If your bill went up because the rate went up, the assessor cannot help you. If it went up because the appraisal went up, you have appeal rights.

sections.h2: Who sets the value and who collects the tax?
sections.html:
Two separate offices handle a Tennessee property tax bill. The county assessor of property appraises and classifies the parcel. The county trustee, or a city collecting official inside a city, collects the money. State law keeps those jobs apart on purpose, so the person who values your house never sets your rate.

  • The assessor appraises real estate, tracks ownership and boundary changes, and must verify certain facts on real estate sales with the buyer or seller.
  • The county commission and city governing bodies set the tax rates.
  • The State Board of Equalization writes the procedures assessors follow and hears appeals that go past the county level.
  • The Comptroller's Division of Property Assessments monitors assessors and supports them during reappraisal.

Every county revalues all real property on a four, five or six year cycle. Between those revaluations the appraisal generally stays put unless something changes on the parcel, such as a new building, an addition or a demolition. The assessor sends an assessment change notice whenever the value or the classification changes.

sections.h2: What assessment percentages apply to each kind of property?
sections.html:
Residential and farm real property are assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, which is the lowest rate on the state's list. Commercial and industrial property is assessed at 40 percent, business personal property at 30 percent and public utility property at 55 percent. A rental house owned by an individual is still residential property, so a landlord selling a Tennessee rental starts from the same 25 percent.

Tennessee assessment percentages by property class. Source: Tennessee Comptroller, Assessment vs Taxation.
Property classShare of appraised value assessed
Residential25%
Farm25%
Commercial and industrial40%
Business personal property30%
Public utility55%

The Comptroller's own example is a residence appraised at $100,000, which carries an assessed value of $25,000. Because counties reappraise on different cycles, the state also builds an equalization factor from an appraisal ratio study so that property valued in different years is compared fairly.

sections.h2: When are Tennessee property taxes due and when do they go delinquent?
sections.html:
Current year taxes are due on the first Monday in October, and a bill paid by the last day of February is free of interest. March 1 is the delinquency date for the prior year's taxes. The Comptroller's assessment schedule gives the full calendar, with the statute behind each step.

  • January 1: the assessment date. Records must reflect the property as it stood on that day.
  • May 20: assessments should be complete and change notices mailed. This is also the deadline to apply for exemptions.
  • June 1: the county board of equalization meets, except in Shelby County, where it convenes May 1.
  • July: the county sets its tax rate, with the budget adopted by July 1.
  • August 1: general deadline for appeals to the State Board of Equalization.
  • First Monday in October: taxes become due and payable.
  • February 28: last day to pay the preceding year's taxes without interest.
  • March 1: delinquency date.

The bill covers the whole tax year, so a house that sells in spring or summer still has a full year's tax to account for. Ask the county trustee for the current balance before you sign a purchase contract, and ask the closing agent how the year will be split between buyer and seller.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Tennessee property tax assessment?
sections.html:
Start with the county board of equalization, because a disputed assessment generally becomes final if it was never taken there. Contact the county assessor for the process. Some assessors offer an informal review first, but the State Board of Equalization states plainly that an informal review is not an appeal and does not preserve your later rights.

  • County board: the first formal level, a panel of five or more people who hear taxpayer complaints and can change disputed assessments.
  • State Board: file on or before August 1 of the tax year, or within 45 days of the date the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. Filing is through the board's online system.
  • Hearing: a Notice of Hearing goes out at least 60 days ahead, and an Administrative Judge issues a ruling within 90 days of the hearing.
  • Finality: an Initial Decision and Order is typically final 30 days after the signed order if nobody seeks further review.
  • Court: judicial review needs a petition in chancery court within 60 days from when the board's order becomes final.

You carry the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence. The board says the best evidence for a house is sales of comparable properties, with the differences in size, age, condition and location explained. A bare statement that the house is overvalued is generally not enough. An appraisal can be submitted, though the appraiser may be asked to testify.

Some appeals can skip the county board. The State Board lists these situations: no proper notice of an increase, a change notice mailed less than ten days before the county board adjourned, reasonable cause beyond your control, an appeal of an assessor's correction, and written assessor consent for commercial or industrial property. The board cannot accept any appeal after March 1 of the year following the date the appeal period began to run.

sections.h2: Do I have to pay the tax while an appeal is pending?
sections.html:
You must pay at least the undisputed part before the delinquency date. The State Board's appeal page walks through the arithmetic, which starts from the value you claim in good faith, and the county trustee can give you the figure for your parcel. You also have to pay the full amount of any delinquent taxes on the parcel for earlier years, or the appeal can be delayed or dismissed.

If the board later issues a certificate of assessment that leaves you with an underpayment, you owe the difference plus interest. The interest rate is the Federal Reserve composite prime rate minus two points. Penalty and interest that were postponed during an appeal begin to accrue 30 days after the decision becomes final. A refund is issued within 60 days of when the appeal closes, and any added payment is due within 30 days.

sections.h2: What programs lower the tax bill for Tennessee owners?
sections.html:
The state runs a tax relief reimbursement program, counties and cities may adopt a tax freeze for owners 65 and older, and qualifying farm and forest land can use the greenbelt program. The relief program reimburses taxes already paid, so the owner still receives and pays the bill. For 2026 the Comptroller lists an income cap of $38,470 for elderly and disabled applicants, and the application deadline is 35 days after the local delinquency date, which lands in April.

The greenbelt deadline is March 15, and the assessor can explain how a rollback assessment can follow if the land use changes after enrollment. Our Tennessee homestead exemption guide covers the relief and freeze rules in more detail. Property tax relief applies to one residence per tax year, so owners who sell and move should confirm with the trustee how the program treats the new address.

sections.h2: What should I do about tax due before selling a Tennessee house?
sections.html:
Call the county trustee, and the city collecting official if the house is inside a city, and ask for the payoff figure on the parcel. The Tennessee Property Assessment Database shows the appraisal and classification, which helps you spot a wrong classification early. If the house has a pending appeal, the trustee can tell you what has been paid and what remains.

Owners who plan to appeal should know the State Board expects any delinquent taxes from earlier years to be paid in full. An as-is cash buyer will price any open balance into the offer, and you can request an offer from us at any point, including while a bill is open.

faqs.q: What is the Tennessee property tax rate?
faqs.a: There is no single statewide rate. Each county commission and city governing body sets its own rate, stated as dollars per $100 of assessed value, and a residence is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value. The Comptroller publishes local tax rates, and the county trustee can tell you the combined rate for your address.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal a Tennessee assessment?
faqs.a: The county board of equalization starts meeting June 1, and the State Board of Equalization deadline is August 1 or 45 days after the county board's notice was sent, whichever is later. Change notices are due out by May 20. The 2026 deadlines have passed, so for the next cycle watch for the change notice and ask your assessor for the county board's date.

faqs.q: Can I appeal because my taxes went up?
faqs.a: Only if the increase comes from the value or classification. The Comptroller says the tax amount is not a valid basis for appeal. A higher rate set by the county commission is not something the assessor or the state board can change.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to appeal?
faqs.a: No. The State Board says you may attend alone or bring a representative such as an attorney or authorized agent. The county assessor's office usually sends a representative, and the Administrative Judge decides only on the evidence presented.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay the bill?
faqs.a: Interest starts after the last day of February, and March 1 is the delinquency date. Penalties and interest keep running unless an appeal is pending and you paid the undisputed portion. Ask the county trustee for the exact balance and payment options on your parcel.
